newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Pressure eases on Asia currencies as Latam suffers.
newsitem.headline: Pressure eases on Asia currencies as Latam suffers.

text.p: Pressure on the embattled currencies of Southeast Asia eased somewhat on Wednesday morning, but traders in the region said they were watching a familiar situation developing in Latin America.
"It's a little eerie. It's not busy here and yet the Latin American markets seem to have had a pretty nervous time overnight," said the head of trading at a European bank in Singapore.

The trader confessed he knew little about Latin American markets. "I'm no expert, but looking at my Reuters (screen) I can see there's been some fun and games. It looks like the contagion has spread over there," he said.

Overnight Brazilian markets came under intense pressure as traders focussed on Brazil's large current accound deficit -- currently standing at 4.2 percent of Gross Domestic Product -- and a currency which some economists say is overvalued.
Brazil's main stock market measure, the Bovespa index, plunged 8.51 percent, its largest fall since January 1995. Brazilian debt traded in New York also fell sharply in active trading.
Analysts said there was no one single item of news which prompted the nervousness.
"There is a psychological snowball that is taking place, because nothing fundamental happened to Brazil today," said Larry Krohn, Latin American economist at UBS Securities in New York.
Other Latin American markets -- which look to Brazil, not Wall Street, for direction -- also suffered with the stock markets in Argentina, Mexico and Venezuela all suffering.
However, Brazil's currency, the real, fell only slightly.
But the head of trading commented, "I see that central bank officials (in Brazil) were playing down the prospects of devaluation. Now where have I heard that before?"
Central bank and government officials from Thailand and the Philippines strenuously denied they were going to devalue their currencies.
However, the currencies of both countries were subsequently allowed to fall in what traders and analysts said were de facto devaluations.
But a trader at an Australian bank, who declined to be identified, said he thought pressure on Asian currencies had largely abated.
"In the last couple of day's movements have been volatile, but you could describe it as range-trading, albeit in pretty large ranges," he said.
"Essentially the market has got it wanted, lower currencies," he added.

At 0245 gmt the Philippine peso was trading at around 29.25 to the dollar, slightly above its opening level of 29.50. Prior to its de facto devaluation last Friday it had been trading at around 26.40.
The Thai baht was trading at around 30 to the dollar onshore, little changed from Tuesday's levels, while the Malaysian ringgit was at 2.5620, also little changed.
The Indonesian rupiah was a shade easier at 2457.00 compared with yesterday's close of around 2447.00.
